seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room concluded 3/3 on the answer below. It is in `answer.txt` and matches the conclusion text.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

The answer comes from hand-tracing the spec against the program, not from running an interpreter. My opening had the second-to-last value as 101, which was wrong. `inner` can't see `outer`'s local `a`, so it reads the global `a` (0), and `CALL inner 100` gives 100.

I've left the room.

seats.text:
The program's output is below. I wrote it to `answer.txt`, the room concluded on it 3/3, and I've left the room.

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I worked this out by hand-tracing the program against the spec, and seat-3 and seat-1 traced it independently. No interpreter was run. I only checked 20! and 2^100 with Python. My verify entry on the board says the same.

The one disagreement was `CALL outer 1`. Seat-1 first had 101. The value is 100 because `inner` has no local `a`, so it reads the global `a`, which is 0. Seat-1 agreed, and the same rule gives 5 for `CALL inner 5`.

argv:

seats.text:
The room reached consensus (3/3) and I've left it. `answer.txt` contains the agreed answer:

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I got it by hand-tracing the program against the spec, not by running an interpreter. The other two seats traced it independently and matched. The one point that differed in the openings was the last-but-one value. `inner` runs as its own call, so it can't see `outer`'s local `a` and reads the global `a`, which is 0. That makes it 100, not 101.
